value.overview: The Rufous-vented Ground-Cuckoo is a large, secretive, ground-dwelling cuckoo of tropical forests. It spends much of its time walking or running through dense understory rather than flying in open areas. Its dark brown body, long tail, cinnamon face, irregular black breast band, and rufous lower belly help identify it. The species is especially difficult to observe because it is shy, occurs at low densities, and depends on extensive, mature forest with little disturbance.
value.classification: The Rufous-vented Ground-Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the ground-cuckoo genus Neomorphus. The Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Neomorphus geoffroyi salvini.
value.identification: This ground-cuckoo is about 48 cm long and has a long tail, long neck, shaggy crest, and strong legs. Adults are mainly dark brown above, with subtle green or purple gloss on the wings, tail, and crest. The face is cinnamon, the underparts are grayish brown becoming warmer and more rufous toward the belly and undertail, and an irregular black band crosses the breast. Juveniles are duller and usually lack the distinct breast band.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama into western Colombia, with other populations extending through parts of the Amazon Basin and eastern Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a very uncommon resident of humid lowland and foothill forests, especially on the Caribbean slope, and may occur locally up to roughly 900 m or higher. It requires mature, largely undisturbed evergreen forest with dense ground cover and is rarely found in heavily altered landscapes. Records are scarce because of its secretive behavior.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, individuals are believed to remain in suitable humid forest year-round, although sightings are highly local and irregular. There is no reliable evidence of regular seasonal migration into or out of the country.
value.breeding: Reliable information on breeding is limited. The species is thought to breed in mature tropical forest, where it probably nests close to the ground or in low vegetation, but details of nest construction, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remain poorly documented. In Costa Rica, confirmed breeding records are scarce or uncertain. Reports of recently fledged young at La Selva Biological Station have suggested local breeding, but these observations should be treated cautiously because the species is difficult to study.
value.dietFeeding: The Rufous-vented Ground-Cuckoo feeds mainly on large ground-dwelling prey, including insects, spiders, scorpions, centipedes, small frogs, and lizards. It may occasionally take seeds or fruit. Like other ground-cuckoos, it can follow army-ant or other ant columns and capture animals flushed by the moving ants. It forages by walking, running, and making short jumps through dense understory and fallen vegetation.
value.behavior: This is a shy, quiet, and elusive bird that usually moves alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. It is more agile on the ground than in sustained flight and often slips through thick vegetation when disturbed. Its dependence on dense forest and its tendency to remain low make it difficult to detect, even where it occurs. Following army-ant swarms may bring it into more visible feeding activity, but encounters remain uncommon.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, mainly because suitable mature forest is being lost and fragmented across its range. Precise population estimates and detailed trend data for Costa Rica are lacking.
conservation.threats: The principal threats are clearing and fragmentation of mature tropical forest, agricultural expansion, roads, logging, fires, and other forms of habitat disturbance. Because the species appears to require large, relatively undisturbed forest blocks and has limited ability to cross extensive nonforest areas, isolated populations may be especially vulnerable. Its rarity and poor detectability also make local declines difficult to measure.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore large blocks of mature forest, particularly lowland and foothill rainforest in Costa Rica. Maintain forest corridors between protected areas, reduce logging and agricultural encroachment, and support effective management of reserves on the Caribbean slope. Careful, standardized surveys can improve knowledge of its distribution and breeding status. Birdwatchers should avoid playback, flushing, or pursuing this exceptionally secretive species and should report well-documented observations to local conservation databases.
